facts.statement: Doliodus is an extinct cartilaginous fish from the Early Devonian period found in what is now New Brunswick, Canada.
facts.quote: Doliodus is an extinct genus of cartilaginous fish known from the Early Devonian period of what is now New Brunswick, Canada.

facts.statement: The genus includes one species originally known only from isolated teeth and fin spines, but later a well-preserved body fossil was assigned to it.
facts.quote: It includes a single named species, referred to either as D. problematicus or D. latispinosus, which was originally described based on isolated teeth and fin spines, but has since had a well-preserved body fossil assigned.

facts.statement: Joseph Whiteaves identified the first material as Doliodus in 1881, naming it Ctenacanthus latispinosus based on isolated fin spines.
facts.quote: The first material that some authors classify as Doliodus was identified by Joseph Whiteaves in 1881, and consists of several isolated fin spines which he identified as a new species in the genus Ctenacanthus, and which he named C. latispinosus.

facts.statement: A 2003 paper by Randall Miller and coauthors assigned a well-preserved fossil specimen (NBMG 10127) to the species Doliodus problematicus.
facts.quote: A 2003 paper published in Nature by Randall Miller and coauthors described a fossilized cartilaginous fish with a well-preserved dentition, skull, fins, and trunk (designated as NBMG 10127) and tooth anatomy similar to that described by Woodward and Traquair in D. problematicus, and these authors assigned this specimen to that species.

facts.statement: All known fossil material for Doliodus originates from the Campbellton Formation in Campbellton, New Brunswick.
facts.quote: The isolated fin spines described by Whiteaves, the teeth described by Woodward and Traquair, and the more complete skeleton all originate from the Campbellton Formation of Campbellton, New Brunswick.

facts.statement: Doliodus lived during the Emsian stage of the Early Devonian, approximately 409 to 397 million years ago.
facts.quote: The site is dated to the Emsian stage of the Early Devonian, making these remains approximately 409-397 million years old.

facts.statement: The genus name Doliodus means 'to trick or deceive' because its tooth crowns closely resemble those of the unrelated genus Diplodus.
facts.quote: According to Traquair, the genus name is derived from the Greek root δόλιος or dolios, meaning to trick or deceive. The name was given because of how closely the tooth crowns of the genus resemble those of the unrelated Diplodus.

facts.statement: According to Michal Ginter, Doliodus teeth have two large pointed cusps and smaller projections called cusplets between them.
facts.quote: Per Michal Ginter, the genus Doliodus encompasses only isolated teeth and tooth-whorls assigned to D. problematicus. These teeth had two large pointed cusps (termed diplodont) and smaller projections called cusplets situated between these.

facts.statement: Doliodus had heterodont dentition with two separate types of teeth in different regions of the mouth.
facts.quote: The dentition of the genus was heterodont, and two separate types of teeth were present in different regions of the mouth.

facts.statement: The preserved head and body of the main specimen are 23 cm long, with an estimated total length of 50 to 75 cm.
facts.quote: The head and body of NBMG 10127 is 23 cm long as preserved, and Miller and coauthors estimated a total length of 50 to 75 cm in their description of the specimen.

facts.statement: The pectoral spines of the main specimen were 5.5 cm long, while the largest isolated spines assigned to the species reach up to 9 cm.
facts.quote: The pectoral spines of this specimen were 5.5 cm long, and the largest isolated spines assigned to D. latispinosus are up to 9 cm long.

facts.statement: Some authors suggest the cartilaginous skeleton of Doliodus may have been reinforced by mineralized tessellations, though this is considered uncertain.
facts.quote: The cartilaginous skeleton of the specimen may have been reinforced by mineralized tessellations like those of modern cartilaginous fish, although their presence is considered uncertain by some authors.

facts.statement: Since the discovery of a more complete specimen, Doliodus has been classified as a member of the family Omalodontidae and order Omalodontiformes.
facts.quote: Since the discovery of the more complete specimen, the genus has been considered a member of the family Omalodontiformes and the family Omalodontidae.

facts.statement: Some authors consider Doliodus to have an uncertain position within Chondrichthyes and have not assigned it to a specific order or family.
facts.quote: It has alternatively been suggested that the genus lacks defining features of the Omalodontiformes, and some authors have considered it as Chondrichthyes incertae sedis (uncertain position) and have not assigned it to an order or family.

facts.statement: Doliodus is generally believed to be part of the stem-group of Chondrichthyes, having diverged earlier than the two living subclasses.
facts.quote: While similarities between the assigned skull of Doliodus and members of the chondrichthyan subclass Elasmobranchii have been suggested, the genus is generally believed to be part of the Chondrichthyes stem-group and to have diverged earlier than the two living subclasses of chondrichthyans.

facts.statement: It is debated whether non-tooth material belongs to Doliodus; some researchers include it in D. latispinosus, while others restrict the genus to only teeth of D. problematicus.
facts.quote: A 2017 study by Carole Burrow and coauthors concluded that the name Doliodus latispinosus was correct due to that species being named earliest. Some subsequent researchers have continued to use the combination D. latispinosus to refer to a single species encompassing teeth, fin spines and skeletal material, while a 2023 paper by paleontologist Michal Ginter has instead questioned the assignment of any non-tooth material to Doliodus and restricted it to only the D. problematicus teeth.

facts.statement: Michal Ginter suggests the articulated material and fin spines may belong to the genus Portalodus or an unnamed intermediate genus, tentatively naming it Portalodus? latispinosus.
facts.quote: Michal Ginter regards the articulated material and fin spines as belonging to either the omalodont genus Portalodus or a yet-unnamed genus with features intermediate between Portalodus and Doliodus, and he refers to the species tentatively as "Portalodus? latispinosus".

facts.statement: Doliodus belongs to the parent group Chondrichthyes.
facts.quote: Parent group: Chondrichthyes

facts.statement: Doliodus lived during the Emsian stage, between 410.62 and 393.47 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Emsian to Emsian (410.62 to 393.47 million years ago)

facts.statement: The genus Doliodus was named by Traquair in 1893.
